name: Space Tourism Price Index
description: A curated compilation of publicly available commercial-spaceflight pricing, verified against official operator sources and maintained by Outer Space Trip.
license_note: CC BY 4.0 applies to this compilation (its selection, arrangement, dating, and maintenance). The underlying prices are public facts sourced from operators; each figure carries its own source.
basis: Per seat unless noted. Lunar and Mars figures are projections, not quotes.

operators.status_note: World View was acquired by Ondas Inc. on April 1, 2026 and is pivoting toward defense surveillance work. No commercial passenger launch date has been announced; the $50,000 fare still sits on a checkout page no longer linked from the site, and its deposit form was returning errors as of August 2026.
operators.status_history: World View missed its 2024 commercial launch target and was acquired by Ondas Inc. (a defense and industrial technology company) on April 1, 2026. Under new ownership, World View is pivoting toward defense and intelligence-surveillance-reconnaissance (ISR) missions; no new commercial passenger launch date has been announced. Its $50,000 fare and $500-per-seat deposit are still published on a checkout page, but that page is no longer linked from the site’s navigation — which now leads entirely with Ondas Sentinel ISR work — and the deposit form was returning errors as of August 2026.

operators.status_note: Space Perspective never flew a paying passenger. Furloughs, a Florida spaceport eviction and a July 2025 sale to Spain’s Eos X Space voided every prior reservation. Its website returned as a full brochure site in November 2026, still with no price, no working booking and no timeline; $125,000 was the last listed fare.
operators.status_history: Space Perspective never operated a single crewed passenger flight. The company furloughed most staff in January 2025, was evicted from its Florida spaceport in April 2025, and was acquired by Spain's Eos X Space in July 2025, voiding all prior reservations. Ticket sales are on hold under the new owner; $125,000 was the last publicly listed fare and no new pricing has been confirmed by a primary or top-tier source. In November 2026 spaceperspective.com returned from a “Launching Soon” placeholder as a full brochure site with no fare, a Book Now button that leads nowhere, no timeline and no mention of Eos X Space, so nothing has changed for a buyer.

operators.status_note: French balloon startup now targeting first public flights in 2027 (slipped from 2026): a six-hour ride to 25 km in its pressurized Altaïr capsule, unveiled near Toulouse in April 2026, fine dining included. Tickets are on sale at €180,000 per guest (~$195,000, cancellation insurance included) with a 20% deposit. Partnered with CNES.
operators.status_history: French luxury balloon startup targeting first public flights in 2026, lifting passengers to 25 km in its pressurized Céleste capsule for a six-hour flight (1.5 h ascent, 3 h at altitude, 1.5 h descent) with fine dining and panoramic views. Two capsule configurations are offered: 4 passengers with 1 pilot, or 6 passengers with 2 pilots. Tickets are on sale at €180,000 per guest (~$195,000, cancellation insurance included), up from €170,000 previously; a 20% deposit is due at booking. Partnered with France's national space agency, CNES. In mid-April 2026 Zephalto unveiled Altaïr, its first commercial capsule (four passengers and one pilot), at its Escalquens workshop near Toulouse; founder Vincent Farret d’Astiès told Usine Nouvelle and Journal du Geek that integration and test flights would follow through summer 2026 with a first commercial flight in mid-to-late 2027, and the company’s own roadmap on zephalto.com now lists “First Zephalto flights open to the public” under 2027. The FAQ still prices a seat at €180,000 (cancellation insurance included, 20% deposit), so the fare is unchanged; the date moved on November 9, 2026.

operators.status_note: Spanish balloon startup whose eight-passenger Aurora capsule targets about 35 km for a four-to-six-hour flight. Its FAQ lists €150,000 per seat (about $165,000), takes no deposit and runs a free waitlist. Five test flights completed since December 2022, none crewed; the FAQ puts the first crewed test in 2027 and commercial flights in 2029.
operators.status_history: Spanish balloon-tourism startup (Madrid and Sarasota, FL) whose Aurora capsule is designed to carry eight passengers and a pilot to about 35 km for a four-to-six-hour flight landing on land under a steerable parachute. The company's FAQ lists the fare at €150,000 per seat (about $165,000; the $164,000 press figure from the April 2024 unveiling was the same euro price at an older rate), takes no deposit, and runs a free waitlist instead of bookings. Halo Space has completed one high-altitude uncrewed flight (India, December 2022; parachute deployed at 37 km) and four parachute landing drops (Mojave, 2023); a 2024 Saudi Arabia test was scrubbed by a crane fault. Its own site targets the next uncrewed series (Flights 07–10) for 2026–2027 in Saudi Arabia and the US, crewed test flights for late 2027 and commercial flights for 2029.

operators.status_note: NS-38 (January 22, 2026) was New Shepard’s last tourist flight. On January 30, 2026, Blue Origin announced a pause of at least two years to concentrate on the Blue Moon lunar lander for NASA. The price range shown reflects the most recently reported per-seat figures from the active program.
operators.status_history: NS-38 (January 22, 2026) was New Shepard's last tourist flight. On January 30, 2026, Blue Origin announced a pause of at least two years to concentrate resources on the Blue Moon lunar lander program for NASA. The price range shown reflects the most recently reported per-seat figures from the active program.

operators.status_note: Between fleets. VSS Unity is retired; the first Delta-class ship, Apeiron, is at Spaceport America with test flights ahead. First glide flight expected January 2027, first commercial flight early Q2 2027 (reaffirmed November 12 with Q3 results). The $750,000 seats sold out; a limited tranche is open at $850,000.
operators.status_history: Virgin Galactic is between fleets: VSS Unity is retired from commercial service and flew only non-commercial glide flights from May 2026 as a training proxy for the Delta class. The first Delta commercial spaceflight slipped from Q4 2026 to February 2027 (August 12, 2026, avionics and systems installation) and again to early Q2 2027 (October 26, 2026, avionics software validation); the second Delta ship is expected to begin commercial operations in late Q2 or early Q3 2027. The lead ship, named Apeiron by public vote on October 28, 2026, flew that afternoon from Mesa, Arizona to Spaceport America under the carrier aircraft Eve; software validation, then glide and rocket-powered test flights, come before any passenger flight. On November 12, 2026, with its Q3 results, the company said the first glide flight with Apeiron is expected in January 2027, reaffirmed both commercial-flight targets, opened a limited tranche of seats at $850,000, said more than 100 ticket holders have begun flight preparation, and set a target of 150 spaceflights per year from its first two ships by the end of 2028. The earlier 50 seats at $750,000 (up from the prior $600,000 fare) were oversubscribed and booked out by August 2026. On November 5, 2026 Virgin Galactic announced a three-year agreement with the nonprofit Space for Humanity for three dedicated six-seat charters (up to 18 participants, selected by the nonprofit); no dates, price or financial terms were disclosed. On November 18, 2026 the nonprofit Teachers in Space said it plans to fly two teachers on a Virgin Galactic research flight in 2027 (unnamed, unpriced, still fundraising), and on November 19 Virgin Galactic named University of Florida space biologists Anna-Lisa Paul and Rob Ferl for one of Apeiron’s early NASA-funded research missions; neither moves the fare or the first-flight target.

operators.status_note: Chinese startup that presold two suborbital seats on a 2024 Taobao livestream at 1.5 million yuan (~$210,000) each, for a six-passenger capsule to 100–150 km. Its Nebula-1 rocket flew one landing test (September 2024) and had not reached orbit by November 2026; the capsule has not flown, and no more seats are on sale.
operators.status_history: Chinese startup Deep Blue Aerospace presold its first two suborbital tickets in an October 2024 Taobao livestream at 1.5 million yuan (~$210,000) per seat, for a reusable six-passenger crew capsule reaching 100–150 km altitude with roughly five minutes of weightlessness. The company is running uncrewed test flights through 2026, with commercial suborbital tourism targeted to begin in 2027; no paying passenger has flown yet.

operators.status_note: Beijing-based InterstellOr is preselling seats on its planned six-passenger CYZ1 suborbital capsule at 3 million yuan (~$430,000), with about 20 people signed up. A landing-cushioning test passed in January 2026; no flight of any kind has happened yet. First crewed mission targeted for 2028.
operators.status_history: Beijing-based startup InterstellOr (Chinese: Chuanweizhe) is preselling seats on its planned CYZ1 suborbital capsule — up to six passengers, per the company’s own spec page (early press reports said seven) — at 3 million yuan (~$430,000) per seat, with about 20 people already signed up including actor Johnny Huang Jingyu. The capsule targets the ~100 km Kármán line for 3–6 minutes of weightlessness on a 20–30 minute flight. InterstellOr passed a 2024 feasibility review and completed a landing-cushioning system test in January 2026; no crewed or uncrewed flight has occurred yet, with a first crewed mission targeted for 2028.

operators.status_note: CAS Space, incubated by the Chinese Academy of Sciences (about a fifth owner) and already launching Kinetica-1 and -2, has unveiled the seven-passenger reusable Li Hong-2 capsule: uncrewed debut now Q1 2027; the 2028 passenger target went unrepeated in 2026. Fare 2–3 million yuan (~$280,000–$420,000); no tickets on sale.
operators.status_history: CAS Space (Guangzhou-based, majority-owned by the Chinese Academy of Sciences and already flying its Kinetica-1 orbital rocket) has announced a reusable suborbital ‘space-traveler’ capsule seating seven passengers, targeting a first crewed flight to the edge of space around 2028 after an uncrewed vehicle debut planned for 2027. Tickets are expected to be priced at 2–3 million yuan (~$280,000–$420,000) per seat. No tickets have gone on sale and no crewed flight has occurred yet; the fare is the company’s announced expected range, not a booked price. The company has also floated a launch-every-100-hours model from a planned aerospace theme park.

operators.status_note: Haven-1, Vast’s commercial station, targets a Q1 2027 launch, with a July 2026 update confirming the schedule. NASA selected Vast for its sixth private ISS mission (no earlier than summer 2027), and a $500 million funding round closed in March 2026. No public fare; seats are sold by direct inquiry.
operators.status_history: Haven-1, Vast’s commercial space station, is targeting a Q1 2027 launch after delays from the original 2026 target; a July 2026 progress update confirms the schedule remains on track following completion of key integration and testing milestones. NASA selected Vast for its sixth private astronaut mission to the ISS (NET summer 2027, announced February 2026). France and the UK have signed agreements for seats. Vast closed a $500 million funding round in March 2026 ($300M Series A equity plus $200M debt, led by Balerion Space Ventures). The first crewed station mission (Vast-1) follows Haven-1’s launch and has an announced crew member, ESA reserve astronaut Arnaud Prost. No public per-seat fare; seats are sold by direct inquiry at fly@vastspace.com.

operators.status_note: Voyager Technologies, developer of the Starlab station (prospective ~2029 launch), was selected by NASA for its seventh private astronaut mission. VOYG-1 would fly four people to the ISS on a SpaceX Dragon for up to 14 days, no earlier than 2028. No public fare; seats are sold by direct inquiry.
operators.status_history: Voyager Technologies — developer of the Starlab commercial space station (a Voyager / Airbus / Nanoracks / Lockheed Martin consortium, with a prospective ~2029 launch) — was selected by NASA for its seventh Private Astronaut Mission in 2026. The mission, VOYG-1, will fly a crew of four to the ISS aboard a SpaceX Dragon for up to 14 days, no earlier than 2028 — Voyager’s first crewed private mission. Like other private-astronaut and station seats it is sold by direct inquiry with no public per-seat fare; the flight doubles as commercial-crew training and revenue toward the Starlab station.

operators.status_note: Space Adventures has no active orbital tourism bookings: its Soyuz-to-ISS program has been dormant since its last tourist flight in 2021, with seat availability constrained as Russia winds down ISS participation.

Ax-4 flew June 25 to July 15, 2025. Axiom’s missions page lists Ax-5 as a 14-day mission no earlier than January 2027, and the company describes itself as the only one so far authorized to fly private ISS missions. The ~$55 million per-seat figure dates from Ax-1 (2022); current pricing is not published.
operators.status_history: Ax-4 launched June 25, 2025 and splashed down July 15 after an ISS stay. Axiom’s own missions page lists Ax-5 as a 14-day mission launching no earlier than January 2027; NASA selected Axiom for it in January 2026. Axiom describes itself as the only company so far authorized to fly private missions to the ISS. The ~$55 million per-seat figure derives from Ax-1 (2022) reporting; Axiom does not publish current pricing publicly.
